title: Leave-one-out cross-validation
summary: Leave each point out once, refit n times, and average the squared test residuals. For a linear fit the residual is the ordinary residual divided by 1 minus the hat-matrix leverage. The estimate has low bias and high variance, and it is k-fold with k equal to n.
intuition:
Leave-one-out cross-validation uses the sample twice without training on the point it scores. There are $n$ folds. Fold $i$ holds out point $i$, fits on the other $n-1$ points, and records the error of that fit on the held-out point. Each point is tested once. The LOOCV mean squared error is the average of those $n$ squared residuals. This is $k$-fold cross-validation with $k=n$.

For ordinary linear regression the $n$ refits can be read off the single full-data fit. If $H=X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top$ is the hat matrix of the full sample and $h_{ii}$ is its $i$th diagonal entry, the residual from the fit that excluded point $i$ is
$$y_i-\hat y_{(-i)}=\frac{y_i-\hat y_i}{1-h_{ii}}.$$
The numerator is the ordinary residual. The leverage $h_{ii}$ is between $0$ and $1$ for a linear model with a full-rank design, and the diagonal sums to the number of columns of $X$. A point with leverage near $1$ is almost able to pull the fitted hyperplane onto itself; the formula divides by a small number and the leave-one-out residual blows up. If $h_{ii}=1$ the denominator is zero and the shortcut does not apply.

The training set in each fold has size $n-1$, almost the size of the whole sample, so as an estimate of the test error of a fit on $n-1$ points the procedure has low bias. The $n$ training sets overlap in $n-2$ points, so the $n$ residuals are strongly dependent and the estimate of the error has high variance. Doing it naively costs $n$ fits. The hat-matrix shortcut is special to linear smoothers. A tree or a neural net really is refit $n$ times. And the shortcut is not a licence to scale the features on all $n$ rows first: a preprocessor is part of the fit, so the held-out row must not enter it.

definitions.body: One of $n$ folds. Fold $i$ trains on every point except $i$ and tests on $i$. The model is refit for each $i$. Each point is the test point exactly once.
For a linear fit, $H=X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top$ and $\hat y=Hy$. The leverage of row $i$ is the diagonal entry $h_{ii}$. With an intercept column, $X$ includes a column of ones.
The difference $y_i-\hat y_{(-i)}$ between the held-out response and the prediction from the fit that excluded $i$. For a linear fit it equals $(y_i-\hat y_i)/(1-h_{ii})$.
The mean of the $n$ squared leave-one-out residuals. It estimates test error. Relative to a fit trained on $n-1$ points it has low bias and, because the folds overlap so heavily, high variance.

formulas.name: Hat matrix
formulas.note: $X$ has full column rank and includes a column of ones when the line has an intercept. The trace of $H$ equals the number of columns.

formulas.name: LOO residual
formulas.note: Linear smoothers only. The numerator is the full-data residual. The identity is not a shortcut for a tree or a neural net.

formulas.name: LOOCV MSE
formulas.note: LOOCV is $k$-fold cross-validation with $k=n$. Low bias as an estimate of test error, high variance, and $n$ fits unless the linear shortcut applies.

properties: There are $n$ folds and $n$ refits. Each point is held out once and is absent from the fit that is asked to predict it.
For linear regression the shortcut uses only the full-data residuals and the diagonal of $H$. It matches the explicit refits, which the three-point example below checks term by term.
Leverages satisfy $0\le h_{ii}\le 1$ in the usual full-rank linear model, and $\sum_i h_{ii}$ equals the number of columns of $X$. A leverage of $1$ makes the denominator zero.
As an estimate of the test error of training on $n-1$ points, LOOCV has low bias. The estimate itself has high variance because consecutive training sets differ by only one point.
The procedure is expensive when each fit is expensive: $n$ of them. The linear shortcut does not extend to nonlinear models.
A scaling step is part of the fit. Computing the scale from all $n$ rows lets the held-out point influence the model that is then scored on it.

examples.title: Three points, intercept, and the hat diagonal
examples.prompt: Fit a line with intercept to $(x,y)=(0,1)$, $(1,3)$, $(2,2)$. Compute the leverages, the leave-one-out residuals, and the LOOCV mean squared error.
steps: The design has rows $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$. Then $X^\top X=\begin{pmatrix}3&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix}$, determinant $6$, and $(X^\top X)^{-1}=\tfrac16\begin{pmatrix}5&-3\\-3&3\end{pmatrix}$. The leverages are $h_{11}=\tfrac56$, $h_{22}=\tfrac13$, $h_{33}=\tfrac56$. They sum to $2$, the number of columns.
With $y=(1,3,2)^\top$, the normal equation gives intercept $\tfrac32$ and slope $\tfrac12$, so fitted values are $1.5$, $2$, and $2.5$. Full-data residuals are $-\tfrac12$, $1$, and $-\tfrac12$.
Divide by $1-h_{ii}$: $(-\tfrac12)/(\tfrac16)=-3$, $1/(\tfrac23)=\tfrac32$, and $(-\tfrac12)/(\tfrac16)=-3$. Squared residuals are $9$, $\tfrac94$, and $9$. Their mean is $(81/4)/3=27/4$.
examples.answer: Leave-one-out residuals are $-3$, $\tfrac32$, and $-3$. The LOOCV mean squared error is $\tfrac{27}{4}$.

examples.title: The same residuals by deleting each point
examples.prompt: Refit the line three times, each time dropping one of $(0,1)$, $(1,3)$, $(2,2)$, and compare with the shortcut.
steps: Drop $(0,1)$. The remaining points $(1,3)$ and $(2,2)$ give slope $(2-3)/(2-1)=-1$ and intercept $4$. The prediction at $x=0$ is $4$. The residual is $1-4=-3$.
Drop $(1,3)$. The points $(0,1)$ and $(2,2)$ give slope $\tfrac12$ and intercept $1$. The prediction at $x=1$ is $1.5$. The residual is $3-1.5=\tfrac32$.

Drop $(2,2)$. The points $(0,1)$ and $(1,3)$ give slope $2$ and intercept $1$. The prediction at $x=2$ is $5$. The residual is $2-5=-3$. All three match the hat-matrix shortcut, so the mean of the squared residuals is again $\tfrac{27}{4}$.
examples.answer: Explicit refits reproduce residuals $-3$, $\tfrac32$, $-3$. The shortcut did not change the LOOCV mean squared error $\tfrac{27}{4}$.

traps: Dividing the full-data residual by $h_{ii}$, or by $1+h_{ii}$, instead of by $1-h_{ii}$. At the first point the residual $-\tfrac12$ divided by $1-\tfrac56=\tfrac16$ is $-3$, not $(-\tfrac12)/(\tfrac56)=-\tfrac35$.
Averaging the three full-data residuals and calling that LOOCV. Those residuals are $-\tfrac12$, $1$, $-\tfrac12$. The leave-one-out residuals are $-3$, $\tfrac32$, $-3$.
Using the linear shortcut on a decision tree or a neural net. The identity needs a linear smoother. Other models are refit once per held-out point.
Describing LOOCV as a low-variance estimate. The bias, relative to training on $n-1$ points, is low. The variance of the estimate is high because the training sets almost coincide.
Standardising all $n$ rows, then holding one row out of the linear fit only. The held-out row already entered the scale. The preprocessor is refit on the $n-1$ training rows.
python:
# Line with intercept on (0,1), (1,3), (2,2). LOOCV MSE is 27/4.
xs = [0, 1, 2]
ys = [1.0, 3.0, 2.0]

def fit(pairs):
    n = len(pairs)
    mx = sum(x for x, _ in pairs) / n
    my = sum(y for _, y in pairs) / n
    sxx = sum((x - mx) ** 2 for x, _ in pairs)
    sxy = sum((x - mx) * (y - my) for x, y in pairs)
    slope = sxy / sxx
    return my - slope * mx, slope

residuals = []
for i in range(3):
    train = [(xs[j], ys[j]) for j in range(3) if j != i]
    intercept, slope = fit(train)
    pred = intercept + slope * xs[i]
    residuals.append(ys[i] - pred)
assert residuals == [-3.0, 1.5, -3.0]
mse = sum(r * r for r in residuals) / 3
assert abs(mse - 27 / 4) < 1e-12
print(mse)

questions.stem: A linear fit has full-data residual $-\tfrac12$ at a point whose leverage is $\tfrac56$. The leave-one-out residual is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $-3$.

Divide by $1-h_{ii}=1-\tfrac56=\tfrac16$. Then $(-\tfrac12)/(\tfrac16)=-3$. Option C divides by the leverage itself. Option D multiplies the residual by $1-h_{ii}$ instead of dividing.

questions.stem: For the design with rows $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$, and $(1,2)$, the three leverages are $\tfrac56$, $\tfrac13$, and $\tfrac56$. Their sum equals
options: $1$, because $H$ is a projection of rank $1$
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $2$.

$\tfrac56+\tfrac13+\tfrac56=\tfrac{5}{6}+\tfrac{2}{6}+\tfrac{5}{6}=2$. The trace of the hat matrix equals the rank, here the two columns (intercept and slope). It is not the sample size, and it is not the sum of residuals.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true of leave-one-out cross-validation?
options: For a linear fit, $y_i-\hat y_{(-i)}=(y_i-\hat y_i)/(1-h_{ii})$.
As an estimate of test error it has low bias and high variance.
The point held out is included in the fit that produces its leave-one-out prediction.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

Each of the $n$ points is a test fold of its own, which is $k$-fold with $k=n$. The displayed residual identity is the linear shortcut, with $h_{ii}$ from the full-data hat matrix. Training sets of size $n-1$ keep the bias low and the heavy overlap keeps the variance of the estimate high. D is false: the held-out point is not a training row of the fit that predicts it.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true when LOOCV is computed from a linear fit?
options: The shortcut needs the full-data residuals and the diagonal of $H=X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top$.
If some $h_{ii}=1$, the denominator $1-h_{ii}$ is zero.
The same algebraic shortcut applies to an unpruned decision tree with no change.
Fitting a scaler on all $n$ rows, then deleting one row only from the linear fit, still lets the held-out row affect the score.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and D**.

The identity is $(y_i-\hat y_i)/(1-h_{ii})$, so a leverage of $1$ makes it undefined. A tree is not a linear smoother, so C is false: the tree is refit $n$ times. A scaler fit on every row, including the row about to be scored, has already used the test point.

questions.stem: A line with intercept is fit to $(0,1)$, $(1,3)$, and $(2,2)$. The three leave-one-out residuals are $-3$, $\tfrac32$, and $-3$. The LOOCV mean squared error is $m$. Enter $4m$.
questions.solution:
The answer is **27**.

The squared residuals are $9$, $\tfrac94$, and $9$. Their sum is $\tfrac{36}{4}+\tfrac{9}{4}+\tfrac{36}{4}=\tfrac{81}{4}$. The mean is $m=(\tfrac{81}{4})/3=\tfrac{27}{4}$. Therefore $4m=27$.
